nameStory: The name "buffalo-nut" likely comes from the plant's large, egg-shaped nuts that early settlers thought resembled something a buffalo might eat. It's also called "oil nut" because the seeds contain oils that were once extracted for various uses, though the plant is actually quite toxic despite its nutty appearance.
description: Buffalo-nut is an uncommon shrub that grows up to 13 feet tall in the shaded understory of eastern forests. It has simple, oval leaves and produces small, greenish flowers followed by distinctive egg-shaped nuts. What makes this plant truly unusual is that it's a "vampire" plant - while it can photosynthesize like other green plants, it also secretly taps into the roots of nearby trees and shrubs to steal nutrients.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Large, egg-shaped nuts about an inch long with a smooth, pale green to yellowish surface that feels waxy to the touch - these distinctive fruits are the plant's calling card

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Simple, oval leaves arranged alternately along the stems, with a soft, slightly fuzzy texture on the undersides and prominent veining

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Grows as a multi-stemmed shrub reaching 6-13 feet tall, typically found lurking in the shaded understory rather than in sunny openings

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small, inconspicuous greenish flowers that appear in spring, clustered along the branches and easily overlooked among the foliage

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Smooth, grayish bark on younger stems that becomes slightly rougher with age, but never develops deep furrows

habitat: Buffalo-nut thrives in rich, moist soils of deciduous and mixed forests, particularly in mountainous areas of western New England. Look for it in shaded ravines, north-facing slopes, and woodland edges where it can find both the shade it prefers and plenty of host plants to parasitize. It's most commonly found in the same forests as maples, oaks, and other hardwood trees whose roots it can tap into.

seasonality.spring: Small greenish flowers appear in late spring, though they're easily missed among the emerging leaves. New leaves unfurl with a soft, fresh appearance.
seasonality.summer: Foliage is fully developed and the distinctive egg-shaped fruits begin forming and growing throughout the summer months.
seasonality.fall: The characteristic nuts reach full size and turn yellowish, making this the best time for identification. Leaves may turn yellow before dropping.
seasonality.winter: Bare branches reveal the shrub's multi-stemmed growth pattern, and any remaining nuts on the ground can help confirm past presence.

funFact: Buffalo-nut is nature's secret thief - it extends tiny root connections called haustoria underground to literally plug into its neighbors' root systems and siphon off water and nutrients, making it one of New England's few parasitic plants that still looks completely normal and green!
confusionNotes: The large, smooth nuts might be confused with buckeyes, but buffalo-nut fruits are single nuts rather than the spiky capsules that split open to reveal buckeye seeds. Remember: buffalo-nuts are "loners" - single smooth nuts, while buckeyes come in prickly packages.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a "nut," the seeds are actually toxic and shouldn't be eaten, unlike true edible nuts. The plant belongs to the sandalwood family, making it a distant relative of the fragrant sandalwood trees, though our New England species lacks that characteristic scent.
compareHints: Buffalo-nut is the only member of its genus in North America, making it unique in New England. Within the sandalwood family, it's distinguished from its relatives by being a temperate forest shrub rather than a tropical tree, and by its large, conspicuous nuts rather than small berries or drupes typical of other family members.
